items.title: docs(skill): cmd/skill_cli.md tells agents to run non-existent "proposal get --json"
items.body:
## Summary

The embedded agent skill `cmd/skill_cli.md` (v0.5.0) instructs agents to poll
proposal status with a command that does not exist:

> `agent-vault vault proposal get <id> --json` every 3s for the first 30s, then every 10s...

Neither the subcommand nor the flag is valid, so the poll loop never works.

## Reproduction

```bash
agent-vault vault proposal create --name brave-search --host api.search.brave.com \
  --auth-type api-key --api-key-key BRAVE_SEARCH_API_KEY \
  --api-key-header x-subscription-token -m "test" --json
# -> {"id":1,"approval_url":"...","status":"pending"}

agent-vault vault proposal get 1 --json
# Error: unknown flag: --json   (`get` is not a subcommand either)
```

## Actual CLI surface (v0.39.0; unchanged on main / v0.40.0)

- `agent-vault vault proposal show <number>` - no `--json`
- `agent-vault vault proposal list [--status ...]` - no `--json`
- `--json` exists only on `proposal create` and `vault discover`

## Impact

An agent following the skill verbatim gets `Error: unknown flag: --json`, so
status polling silently fails and the agent stalls until its own 10-minute
timeout. Reproduced while wiring the Brave Search API through a proposal.

## Location

`cmd/skill_cli.md` line 75.

## Suggested fix

```diff
-2. Poll `agent-vault vault proposal get <id> --json` every 3s for the first 30s, then every 10s. Stop after 10 minutes — the proposal may have expired.
+2. Check status with `agent-vault vault proposal show <number>` (or `agent-vault vault proposal list`) until it reads `applied`. Stop after 10 minutes — the proposal may have expired.
```

If JSON output is wanted for programmatic polling, add `--json` to `show`/`list`; otherwise the doc fix above is sufficient.

items.title: feat: clone an existing vault so a new one does not need to be reconfigured
items.body:
## Problem

Creating a second vault that should behave like an existing one means re-entering the whole configuration: credentials, service rules (host, auth type, substitutions), unmatched-host policy, and credential-store settings. `agent-vault vault create` always starts empty. There is no clone or duplicate path in the CLI or the UI.

This shows up in the [use cases](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault#use-cases), where several agents or environments share the same broker rules but should stay in separate vaults:

- A second coding agent, or a personal vault and a work vault, with the same Anthropic and GitHub service rules
- Another all-purpose agent (OpenClaw, Hermes) that should start from an already-working vault
- A new project or ephemeral-sandbox vault that should inherit the same service map instead of being built proposal by proposal

## Proposal

Add a clone operation in the UI and the CLI, for example:

```bash
agent-vault vault clone <source> <new-name>
```

Copy into the new vault:

- Service definitions (name, host/path, auth type, substitutions, enabled flag)
- Credential slots and values for the built-in store, or the Infisical credential-store binding, without minting a second set of upstream secrets
- Vault settings such as `unmatched_host_policy`

Do not copy:

- Agents, members, and session tokens. The new vault should get its own grants.
- Request logs and proposals

A `--services-only` flag would help when the new vault should reuse the rules but hold different credential values, for example personal and work keys on the same hosts.

## Related

#334 asks for services as a top-level entity so agents compose services and vaults. That removes duplication at the model level. Clone is the smaller step: keep the current per-vault model, and stop making operators rebuild an identical vault by hand.

items.title: CI: add govulncheck job - 3 reachable vulnerabilities currently on main
items.body:
## Summary

CI currently has no dependency vulnerability scan. `go-test`, `go-lint` (gosec), `frontend-build`, `go-mod-tidy`, and `sdk-ts` all pass, yet a `govulncheck` run against today's `main` finds **3 reachable vulnerabilities from 2 indirect modules** — all with fixes available, none caught by any CI job.

## Evidence

  Scan run 2026-10-05 against `main` (govulncheck v1.8.0, default vuln.go.dev DB), symbol-level analysis:

  | Vuln | Module | Issue | Fixed in |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | [GO-2026-6348](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6348) | `google.golang.org/grpc@v1.79.3` | Heap exhaustion (OOM) via HTTP/2 DATA frame fragmentation | v1.83.1 |
  | [GO-2026-6061](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-6061) | `google.golang.org/grpc@v1.79.3` | xDS RBAC authorization engine + HTTP/2 transport server | v1.82.1 |
  | [GO-2026-5506](https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-5506) | `go.opentelemetry.io/otel@v1.39.0` | Excessive allocations from multi-value baggage headers | v1.41.0 |

  All three are indirect dependencies pulled in through `github.com/infisical/go-sdk` (GCP IAM auth path). Reachable via:
  `internal/ca/soft.go`, `internal/infisical/client.go`, `internal/telemetry/telemetry.go`.

## Current coverage gap

- **Dependabot** bumps versions weekly (with cooldowns — by design, deliberately behind), and only when a newer version exists. It does not alert on *reachable* vulnerabilities in the currently-pinned versions, and nothing blocks a PR that introduces one.
- **gosec** (via golangci-lint) covers source-level issues in first-party Go code only — not the dependency graph.
- Advisory patches so far have been reactive and manual (#141, #389). #108 covered supply-chain hardening (signing, provenance, digest pinning) but not vulnerability scanning.

For a credential broker, a merged PR silently introducing a reachable vulnerability in `grpc`/`otel`/`x/crypto` is a meaningful failure mode.

## Proposal

Add a `go-vulncheck` job to `ci.yml`, run on every PR and push to `main` (unconditionally, same rationale as `go-test` — path-gating a security check invites filter drift). Sketch, matching existing job conventions:

```yaml
    go-vulncheck:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@<sha> # v7.0.1
          with:
            persist-credentials: false
        - uses: actions/setup-go@<sha> # v6.5.0
          with:
            go-version-file: go.mod
        # go:embed all:webdist needs the directory present at analysis time;
        # real Vite output is validated by the frontend-build job.
        - name: Stub webdist for go:embed
          run: |
            mkdir -p internal/server/webdist
            printf '<!doctype html><title>ci-stub</title>' > internal/server/webdist/index.html
        - uses: golang/govulncheck-action@<sha>
          with:
            go-package: ./...
```

Also add it to ci-summary's needs so it gates merges.

Notes:
  - Symbol-level mode (the default) only fails on vulnerabilities the code actually reaches — low false-positive rate, no module-graph noise.
  - Runtime cost is roughly one go build of the module graph.

The three vulnerabilities above are fixed by bumps tested locally (go build + full go test ./... pass):

- google.golang.org/grpc     v1.79.3 → v1.84.0
- go.opentelemetry.io/otel  v1.39.0 → v1.47.0

Running `grype` on SBOM built with `syft` also found two module-level issues with `klauspost` and `x/crypto`. 
Happy to send the dependency-bump and the CI job as separate PRs, whichever order you prefer.

items.title: Substitution can't match placeholders inside HTTP Basic auth (breaks per-agent tokens for git over HTTPS)
items.body:
## Problem

Substitutions can't reach a placeholder that the client sends inside an HTTP Basic `Authorization` header. The client base64-encodes `username:password` before the request leaves, so a placeholder used as the password (`__my_token__`) goes over the wire as part of an opaque base64 string. A `header`-surface substitution never sees the literal.

The most common case is **git over HTTPS**. GitHub (and most git hosts) only accept Basic auth for git operations. A token or Bearer header is rejected. So an agent that should hold only a placeholder can't use plain `git` through the broker with per-agent credentials. The typed `basic` auth type does work, but it injects one credential for every agent that reaches the host, which rules out per-agent tokens on the same host.

## Repro

1. Service `github.com`, `auth: passthrough`, with the substitution `{key: GH_TOKEN_A, placeholder: __gh_token_a__, in: [header]}`.
2. `git -c credential.helper= ls-remote https://x-access-token:__gh_token_a__@github.com/<org>/<private-repo>.git`, run through the broker (`agent-vault run --`).
3. The result is a 401, because the Basic header carries `base64("x-access-token:__gh_token_a__")` and never matches the placeholder.

(`gh api` with `Authorization: Bearer __gh_token_a__` against `api.github.com` works as expected. The limitation is specific to Basic auth.)

## Proposal

Let a substitution optionally decode Basic credentials. For example, a new surface `basic_auth`, or a flag on the `header` surface. When `Authorization: Basic <b64>` is present, the broker would decode it, substitute placeholders in the username and password, and re-encode. The scoping model stays the same. The operator opts in per substitution, and nothing is decoded unless it's declared.

This would make placeholders work transparently for git, and for any tool that uses Basic auth (many self-hosted APIs, registries and package indexes). That is the one mainstream auth shape substitutions can't cover today.

items.title: vault run --isolation container fails when docker on PATH is podman in docker-compat mode
items.body:
Podman 5+ speaks the docker CLI protocol (and on a few distros installs a docker symlink to podman). Running vault run --isolation container against that fails:

```
$ docker version
Client: Podman Engine
...
$ agent-vault vault run --isolation container -- <agent>
Error: create docker network: docker network inspect agent-vault-07494dd86c6aea30: exit status 125
```

Why
internal/isolation/network.go:77 extracts the gateway via:
`--format "{{range .IPAM.Config}}{{.Gateway}}{{end}}"`

Podman's network inspect JSON shape is different — gateway is at .subnets[].gateway, no IPAM.Config wrapper. The CLI's Go template engine returns exit 125 with can't evaluate field IPAM in type interface {} and the create flow bails out.
The "create docker network:" prefix is also misleading: the network actually creates fine, it's the post-create inspect that fails, then the deferred docker network rm runs.
Secondary bug
parseNetworkInspect only matches PascalCase keys (Created, Containers). Podman emits lowercase (created, containers), so on podman info.Created.IsZero() is always true and PruneStaleNetworks would consider every network stale and prune it immediately — defeating the grace window. Silent, only visible as "my container lost its network partway through".
Suggested fix
Switch both --format inspects to {{json .}} (same template inspectNetworkInfo already uses) and parse in Go, accepting both shapes:
- .IPAM.Config[].Gateway (docker classic)
- .Subnets[].gateway (docker 25+ normalized / podman)
First non-empty gateway wins. Same dual-casing for Created/created and Containers/containers in the prune parser.

I have a fork/pr ready if you like

items.title: Request Logs page accumulates rows and DOM nodes without bound — full-table re-render on every 3s poll freezes Chrome on active vaults
items.body:
### Summary

The Request Logs page (`LogsView`) tails new rows every 3 seconds and prepends
them into state **without ever trimming**, and `DataTable` renders every row it
is given (no windowing, no memoization). While the page stays open, DOM nodes
and heap grow linearly with proxied traffic, and every poll that brings fresh
rows re-renders the **entire table**. On a vault carrying real agent workload,
the tab balloons to hundreds of thousands of DOM nodes, the main thread blocks
for hundreds of ms on every poll, and the browser eventually freezes —
reproducibly, with the page taking the rest of Chrome down with it.

The server side of the contract is fine; this is purely client-side
accumulation + rendering (details in Impact).

### Where

- `web/src/components/LogsView.tsx` — `pollNew()`:
  ```ts
  if (fresh.length > 0) {
    setRows((prev) => [...fresh, ...prev]);   // only ever prepended, never trimmed
  }
  ```
  `rows` grows without bound for as long as the page is open. `pollMs` defaults
  to 3000.
- `web/src/components/LogsView.tsx` — the polling effect:
  ```ts
  const id = setInterval(() => { pollNew(); }, pollMs);
  ```
  No in-flight guard, so a slow response lets overlapping polls stack up.
- `web/src/components/DataTable.tsx`:
  ```ts
  data.map((item, index) => ( ... ))          // renders all rows, no windowing
  ```
  No virtualization and no `React.memo` anywhere in the path; the `columns`
  array and its per-row render closures are rebuilt on every render.

### Impact (measured)

Reproduced on an isolated instance (server `0.39.3`, commit `e9515fe`;
`LogsView.tsx` is byte-identical on `main` as of 2026-09-24) with synthetic
traffic pushed through the proxy and the real management UI in headless Chrome,
sampled over CDP (original symptom observed in desktop Chrome):

| traffic                        | rows accumulated in page | DOM nodes | JS heap | main-thread block per 3s poll        |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------|-----------|---------|--------------------------------------|
| 2 req/s × 3 min                | 341                      | 4,919     | 9 MB    | —                                    |
| ~17 req/s × ~2.5 min           | 2,797                    | 39,303    | 22 MB   | —                                    |
| continued                      | 3,909                    | 54,871    | 35 MB   | 87–257 ms (12 long tasks / 20 s)     |
| continued                      | 5,309                    | 74,471    | 39 MB   | 128–306 ms (15 long tasks / 25 s)    |

- Growth is **strictly linear**: ≈14 DOM nodes/row and ≈8–9 KB JS heap/row;
  per-poll main-thread block scales with row count (CPU profile lands in React
  reconciliation + GC).
- The server-side retention cap (default 10k rows/vault, `internal/requestlog/retention.go`)
  protects the database but **not an open page**: the `after` cursor only moves
  forward, so the browser keeps accumulating past the 10k the server keeps.
- Extrapolated (mechanism is linear, constants measured): one agent at 1–2
  req/s with the page left open over a workday → tens of thousands of rows →
  ~500k+ DOM nodes, JS heap 250–500 MB plus Blink DOM-side memory, and
  per-poll main-thread blocks approaching ~1 s every 3 s.
- The "Paused" button stops the bleeding, but "Live" is the default.

For contrast, the server contract is already burst-safe: `handle_logs.go`
returns the *oldest* rows after the `after` cursor (ASC fetch flipped to DESC)
and `latest_id` is the max id within the returned page, so bursts > page size
don't lose rows and poll payloads stay bounded at `limit`. The unboundedness is
entirely in the client's state and rendering.

### Suggested fix

- Cap `rows` in state (e.g. keep the newest ~500–1000 rows) when prepending in
  `pollNew`, and define the interaction with the "Load more" history pagination
  (a cap means the page keeps a bounded live window rather than unbounded
  history).
- Add an in-flight guard to `pollNew` so overlapping polls can't stack.
- Optionally, window the table in `DataTable` — that touches all of its
  consumers, whereas the state cap + poll guard are contained to
  `LogsView.tsx` and are sufficient to stop the unbounded growth.

items.title: credential-store sync reports ok on a fetch that returned zero secrets, and sync health reads ok while the syncer is not running
items.body:
### Summary

Two related gaps in external-store sync health reporting, both hit by a real deployment:

1. **A fetch that returned zero secrets is recorded as a successful sync.** `refresh()` writes `last_sync_status = ok`, advances `last_synced_at`, and logs `infisical sync ok ... keys=0`. Worse, the write path deletes the vault's static credentials *before* inserting the fetched set, so a zero-secret fetch silently **empties** the vault while reporting success.
2. **Nothing ever downgrades that `ok`.** The connect path writes `last_sync_status = ok` at configure time, and when the daemon has no Infisical client at all (missing/incorrect machine-identity env), the syncer never runs, so no failure is ever recorded. A broker that stopped syncing days ago still reports `ok` from `vault credential-store show` / `vault list`, with a `last_synced_at` that looks recent.

Net effect: `last_sync_status` can read `ok` for a broker that has not fetched anything in days, and there is no key count anywhere in the API or CLI to tell the two apart. `last_synced_at` cannot be used as a freshness signal either, because `recordFailure()` deliberately bumps it as retry backoff.

### Version / environment

- `agent-vault version 0.39.1`, sha256 `eed0b29dcdac15b99cdccf6f43bd8297c5da1544a2802d28970edef709b7d844`, Linux amd64.
- Verified against the `v0.39.1` tag; `internal/infisical/sync.go` has not changed since 2026-06-13 (`5e340cd`), and `main` matches what I read.
- SQLite store, Infisical `universal` auth method, Infisical to a self-hosted instance.
- Nothing in this report has been reproduced on a zero-secret upstream path — see *What I could not verify*.

### 1. Zero-secret fetch = destructive success

`internal/infisical/sync.go` `refresh()` ([v0.39.1 L160-L208](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/infisical/sync.go#L160-L208)):

```go
secs, err := s.fetcher.FetchSecrets(ctx, cfg)
if err != nil { s.recordFailure(...); return err }
items, err := EncryptSecrets(secs, s.dek)
...
applied, err := s.store.ReplaceVaultCredentialsForSync(ctx, cs.VaultID, cs.ConfigJSON, items)
...
if err := s.store.UpdateVaultCredentialStoreHealth(ctx, cs.VaultID, store.SyncStatusOK, "", s.clock()); err != nil { ... }
s.logger.Info("infisical sync ok", slog.String("vault_id", cs.VaultID), slog.Int("keys", len(items)))
```

There is no `len(items) == 0` guard: an empty upstream result takes the success path. `ReplaceVaultCredentialsForSync` → `replaceCredentialsTx` ([sql_store.go L364-L370](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/store/sql_store.go#L364-L370)) unconditionally runs

```go
DELETE FROM credentials WHERE vault_id = ? AND type = 'static'
```

and then inserts nothing when `items` is empty. So a fetch that legitimately returns zero secrets (correct project/env, existing but empty secret path, secrets moved to a different path, or secrets all filtered client-side) **wipes the broker's mirror of that vault** and records a healthy sync.

The same pass-through exists at connect time: `prepareInfisicalSnapshot` ([handle_vaults.go L586-L612](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/server/handle_vaults.go#L586-L612)) accepts a zero-secret fetch and stores `last_sync_status: ok`.

### 2. `ok` is written at configure time and never reconciled

- `SetVaultExternalStore` ([sql_store.go L438-L453](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/store/sql_store.go#L438-L453)) hard-codes `last_sync_status = ok` and `last_synced_at = now` in the upsert, and the vault-create response mirrors that ([handle_vaults.go L647-L653](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/server/handle_vaults.go#L647-L653)).
- If the machine identity is missing, `infisical.NewClient` errors, the server logs one startup WARN and never attaches a client ([cmd/server.go L255-L275](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/cmd/server.go#L255-L275)); the periodic syncer is not started at all, so `recordFailure` is never reached for those vaults.
- A manual `sync` on such a server correctly fails with 503 `infisical_not_configured` — but the stored health row keeps saying `ok`, and that stored row is what `vault credential-store show` and `vault list` render. `RefreshOnce` returns `ErrSyncerDisabled` ([sync.go L118-L121](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.1/internal/infisical/sync.go#L118-L121)) without touching health.

Observed in our deployment: one broker ran for ~4 days with no machine-identity vars in its daemon environment. Its journal contained **zero** infisical-related lines for that whole window (no `client ready`, no `syncer disabled`, no sync failure), while `vault credential-store show` reported `Last sync: ok` with a `last_synced_at` from the day the vault was connected. Consumers reading that vault silently got a stale snapshot; we only noticed by diffing key sets against a second broker.

### Impact

`last_sync_status` currently means "the last *attempt* that got as far as the write path succeeded", not "this broker can still reach upstream". For a credential broker that is precisely the field an operator watches, and it is the only sync-health surface exposed.

### Suggested fixes

1. Include a key count in the sync result: `keys_fetched` (and ideally `keys_written`) in the `credential_store` summary and in `vault credential-store sync` output, e.g. `✓ Synced vault "x" (5 keys)`.
2. Treat a zero-secret fetch as failure (or at minimum skip the destructive replace and keep the previous mirror): `last_sync_status = error` with something like `upstream returned 0 secrets`. If a legitimately empty path must be supported, require an explicit opt-in flag.
3. Don't copy the fetch into the credentials table when it is empty; and consider not clearing the previous set before the new one is inserted.
4. On startup, if any vault has an external credential store but no client was attached, mark those rows `error` (`last_sync_error: "infisical not configured on this server"`) instead of leaving the last `ok` in place. Same for `SetVaultExternalStore`: it writes `ok` based on the caller's probe, which is momentarily true but then never re-validated.
5. Separate retry backoff from sync freshness so `last_synced_at` doesn't advance on failure — e.g. a `next_retry_at` column. Today `last_synced_at` is documented in-code as retry backoff, so it cannot be trusted as a freshness signal.

### What I could not verify

- I could not reproduce the zero-secret case end to end, because doing so on a live broker empties a vault that agents are actively reading; I would rather not test that on production. Reading the code above, the path looks unambiguous, and I could not find a test covering an empty fetch (`internal/infisical/sync_test.go` covers reconnect-mid-sync, failure-keeps-stale, and key validation, but not zero keys). Happy to run a patch against a scratch instance if you want confirmation before changing behavior.
- I have not checked whether the SDK can return `([], nil)` from a 401/403 or a transient upstream error; if it can, that widens defect 1 to "upstream is unreachable" rather than "path is empty". Our broker's daemon had no credentials at all, which surfaces as the 503 path in defect 2.

### Why we filed it

Our fix was at the config layer (an `EnvironmentFile` written with a prefixed variable name, so the daemon never saw `INFISICAL_*`). Upstream correctness is the reason for this report: the status field told us everything was fine for four days while a vault served stale credentials, and the log was silent as well. Reporting the two health-reporting gaps is the whole point of this issue — we are not asking you to change the env-var contract.

items.title: Question: portable evidence when Agent Vault request logs leave the broker?
items.body:
Hi — I found Agent Vault while looking at systems where an AI agent’s consequential external action passes through a trusted broker rather than the agent holding credentials directly.

I’m building BoundaryAttest, an experimental open-source project around portable signed evidence at selected trust boundaries:

https://github.com/cullenmeyers/BoundaryAttest

I read through Agent Vault’s current request-brokering and logging model first, and I would **not** want BoundaryAttest to replace the native security model.

Agent Vault already owns the important runtime boundary:

```text
agent
→ authenticated Agent Vault session/token
→ proxy receives outbound HTTP request
→ service rule is matched
→ real credential is resolved/injected
→ authenticated request is sent upstream
→ response returns through the broker
→ non-secret request metadata is recorded
```

The current request record already captures useful facts such as:

- vault ID;
- actor type / actor ID;
- HTTP method;
- target host + path;
- matched service;
- credential key names, never values;
- upstream status;
- latency;
- error code;
- detected authentication scheme/header.

And I like that the logging model deliberately avoids bodies, header values, and query strings.

For normal operation inside one Agent Vault deployment, I don’t see a reason to add another receipt layer.

The boundary I’m interested in is what happens when that evidence leaves Agent Vault.

The request-log `Sink` abstraction already seems designed with that possibility in mind — the current implementation persists locally, while the package comments mention future sinks such as HTTP webhooks or stdout JSONL.

So imagine:

```text
agent attempts GitHub / cloud / payment / other API action
→ Agent Vault brokers the credential
→ Agent Vault records what it observed
→ selected log/evidence is later:
     streamed to a SIEM,
     sent over a webhook,
     put into an incident packet,
     given to a customer/auditor,
     or retained independently
```

At that point, what should the external recipient actually trust?

I see a few possible answers.

### 1. Agent Vault remains the trust endpoint

If consumers should always query the originating Agent Vault instance or its authoritative database, then I think a separate portable signature is unnecessary.

The broker/database remains the source of truth.

### 2. The external logging system becomes authoritative

If logs are streamed into something like a SIEM that provides its own authenticated ingestion, retention, and tamper-evident history, that native evidence may already be the better object to rely on.

In that case I would prefer Agent Vault to send sufficiently precise native metadata and let the downstream system own long-term evidence.

### 3. A specific broker observation needs to survive independently

There may be cases where another party needs to retain a narrow historical statement like:

> this expected Agent Vault signer says actor A, through vault V, caused the broker to issue an authenticated request matching service S to host/path H and observed upstream result R.

That seems closer to a real portable-attestation boundary.

A narrow record could bind something like:

```text
vault_id
actor_type / actor_id
method
host
path
matched_service
credential key names
upstream status
error code
request-log/event ID
timestamp
signer/public-key identity
```

Possibly also an explicit digest/reference to a richer evidence object where one exists.

I would keep the claim intentionally constrained.

It would **not** prove:

- that the agent was entitled to make the business action;
- that the service rule was correct;
- that the external API processed the request truthfully;
- that a 2xx response means the intended real-world effect occurred;
- that Agent Vault itself was uncompromised;
- or that the surrounding request history is complete.

That last point seems particularly important here.

The current `BatchSink` is deliberately non-blocking; records may be dropped if its bounded buffer fills, and insert failures are logged rather than retried indefinitely.

Retention is also intentionally bounded.

So even if a particular request record were signed, I would interpret that only as:

> this specific request observation was attested

not:

> every relevant Agent Vault request is represented in this evidence set.

I would not want a portable evidence layer to accidentally turn best-effort operational logging into a completeness claim.

There’s also another distinction I think matters:

```text
request permitted by broker
≠ credential injected
≠ outbound request dispatched
≠ upstream response observed
≠ intended external side effect occurred
```

A generic `success` field would blur those together.

If Agent Vault ever wanted native portable evidence, I suspect the stronger design might actually be for Agent Vault itself to define/sign the relevant broker-observation object rather than introduce BoundaryAttest as a second format.

BoundaryAttest would only make sense if the useful boundary is specifically the external handoff/export.

So the question I’m trying to validate is:

**Do you expect selected Agent Vault request/broker evidence to be relied on after it leaves the originating deployment, without continued access to Agent Vault or a stronger downstream system of record?**

If yes, would you prefer to make Agent Vault’s native request evidence independently verifiable, or does a separate export/handoff attestation make more sense?

If no, I’d consider BoundaryAttest redundant here.

No implementation request at this stage — I’m mainly trying to distinguish a genuine portable-evidence requirement from operational request logging that is correctly scoped to the broker itself.

items.title: RFC: per-service MITM request filter (out-of-process sidecar)
items.body:
## Summary

A service may name a filter URL. After that service matches, Agent Vault reverse-proxies the live request to the sidecar **before** the destination credential is decrypted. The sidecar returns an ordinary HTTP response, or sends the request back through the MITM proxy with a short-lived continuation token so Agent Vault can attach the credential and talk to the origin.

The sidecar is not an Agent Vault agent. It does not get a long-lived token.

## Why

Today a service means: this host, path, and port get this credential. Some policies need to see the request while the destination secret is still locked (a git push branch check, a call to a protection API, a rewrite). Agent Vault should not grow a rules engine for those cases. It should keep credential management and offer a seam a downstream program can implement.

Straw man: HTTPS `git push`. The sidecar sees `git-receive-pack`, checks whether the branch is protected, and either returns 403 (the PAT is never opened) or continues so Agent Vault attaches the PAT and talks to GitHub.

## Pipeline

Unfiltered services are unchanged: authenticate, rate limit, match and decrypt, inject, forward.

A filtered service splits that in two:

1. Match the service. Do not decrypt.
2. Reverse-proxy the live request to `filter.url`.
3. Decrypt and inject only if a continuation comes back and its bind still holds.

If the sidecar denies, times out, or cannot be reached, the destination secret must not have been opened. A disabled service or no match does not call the sidecar. If the filter machinery is down, ordinary unfiltered proxying still works.

| When | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| No service matches | Honor `unmatched_host_policy`. Same for an agent token or a policy token. |
| Match, no `filter` | Inject the destination credential and forward. |
| Match, `filter` set, `policy_vault` omitted | Do not decrypt. Mint a continuation only. Reverse-proxy to `filter.url`. |
| Match, `filter` set, `policy_vault` set | Do not decrypt. Mint a continuation and a policy token for the named vault. Reverse-proxy with both. |
| Continuation, bind still holds | Skip the sidecar. Resolve the frozen match. Inject onto this request. Forward. |
| Continuation, bind does not hold | 403 (or 400). Do not rewrite the URL, inject, or forward. The token stays valid until `exp`. |

## Config

Operators write an optional `filter` block in service YAML. There is no dashboard, flag, or `vault service filter` subcommand in v1.

```yaml
services:
  - name: github-push
    host: github.com/*/git-receive-pack
    auth:
      type: bearer
      token: GITHUB_TOKEN
    filter:
      url: https://policy.example.com/github-push
      policy_vault: policy
```

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | yes when `filter` is present | Sidecar URL. `https` normally. Literal-loopback `http` is allowed. Any other `http` requires `allow_insecure_private_http: true`. |
| `policy_vault` | no | Vault the policy token is scoped to. Omitted means no policy token. |
| `allow_insecure_private_http` | no | Opt-in for cleartext HTTP to a private sidecar that is not a literal loopback IP. Weaker than TLS. |
| `ca` | no | PEM certificates used as the only TLS roots for this hop. Omit when `https` uses a public CA. Pin it for a private or self-signed sidecar. No system-root fallback and no skip-verify. |

`url` must be absolute `http` or `https` with a host. A path prefix is allowed; the original path and query are appended after it. Reject userinfo, fragment, query, any other scheme, non-loopback `http` without the insecure flag, and `ca` on an `http` URL. `ca` must be at least one certificate PEM, not a private key.

Omit `policy_vault` for a body-or-headers hop. Set it to the source vault when the sidecar should call other services in that vault. Set it to a different vault to grant that extra access on a smaller vault; the person writing the config must be admin of both.

`vault service add` preserves an omitted filter and clears an explicit `filter: null`. `vault service set` and `clear` replace the list and do not preserve a filter that the file omits. Admin `vault service list` prints the filter, including `ca` when set. Proxy-role reads and `/discover` omit the filter block. The service itself stays visible.

## Hop

Agent Vault is the HTTP client. The sidecar is the origin server for this hop. This is not `CONNECT` and not an absolute-form proxy request.

Preserve method, path (joined with any path prefix on `filter.url`), original query, streaming body, and the original `Host`. Overwrite the hop headers below. Never trust client copies of them. Tokens are headers, never URLs.

| Header | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Original-URL` | Exact original destination URL. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Continuation-Proxy` | Reachable MITM proxy base URL, no credentials. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Continuation-Token` | 30s continuation: `av_cont_` plus an HS256 JWT. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Policy-Proxy` | Present only when `policy_vault` is set. Same idea, no credentials. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Policy-Token` | Present only when `policy_vault` is set. `av_pol_` plus an HS256 JWT. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-CA` | Agent Vault MITM root, base64. The sidecar is not `vault run`. |
| `X-Agent-Vault-Service` | Matched service name. |

Before the sidecar sees the request, delete the header slots that Resolve would overwrite (bearer and basic: `Authorization`; api-key: the configured header, or `Authorization`; custom: every configured output header; passthrough: none), plus `Proxy-Authorization`, `X-Vault`, hop-by-hop headers, and any client `X-Agent-Vault-*`. Do not strip `Authorization` when the service injects a different header.

The callback URL on the hop is `AGENT_VAULT_MITM_ADDR` when set, and otherwise derived from `AGENT_VAULT_ADDR` plus the MITM port. The variable is advertise-only: it does not bind a listener and is not checked against `--host` or `--mitm-port`. An explicit invalid value is fatal at startup. `vault run` dials that host only when the variable is set. When it is unset, `vault run` keeps the host it used to reach the API and the port from `X-MITM-Port`.

Dial policy is separate from `AGENT_VAULT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_RANGES`. `https` without `ca` uses system roots (metadata endpoints stay blocked). `https` with `ca` uses only that PEM pool. Non-loopback `http` requires `allow_insecure_private_http` and may only resolve to loopback, RFC1918, or IPv6 ULA. Redirects are not followed.

A sidecar status, including a denial or a redirect, is copied to the client. Agent Vault does not map a denial to a fixed 403. Hop failure uses the existing proxy envelope (`{"error","message"}`, `X-Agent-Vault-Proxy-Error: true`): `502 filter_unreachable`, `502 filter_misconfigured`, or `504 filter_timeout`. None of those open the destination credential.

Filtered WebSocket upgrades are reverse-proxied to the sidecar with `Upgrade` and `Connection` preserved. A denied upgrade does not Resolve. A continuation upgrade is verified, then resolved and bridged to the origin.

## Tokens

Both tokens are ordinary three-segment HS256 JWTs with a prefix glued on the front (`av_cont_` or `av_pol_`), the same idea as `av_sess_` / `av_agt_`. `exp` is 30 seconds from mint. They are reusable until `exp`, not single-use. A failed bind rejects that request only. `agent revoke` does not cut an already-minted hop JWT. The HMAC key is derived from the DEK after unlock, so every replica that unlocked the same DEK verifies the same tokens. It is not a new stored secret. There is no hop-token table.

Hop JWTs are data-plane credentials only. They are rejected on the control plane (`/discover`, proposals, vault admin). Their vault role is always `proxy`. Verify does not look up the session. Claims carry actor and vault ids for audit and rate limits, which stay with the initiating actor.

The continuation binds method, scheme, authority, escaped path, and raw query, plus a frozen match (which service won, and the non-secret auth and substitution shape). The bind is checked at admission, including CONNECT authority before hijack. After a successful bind, ordinary origin body, first-header, and WebSocket idle budgets apply. The body comes from the sidecar. The sidecar may not change the URL. Resolve uses the frozen match and reads current credential values. It does not run Match again. Unknown frozen-match versions fail closed before any credential read.

The policy token does not carry that frozen match. Presenting it does not inject the hop-start destination credential. A new request with the policy token follows the same pipeline in the named vault, including another filtered hop. A deleted vault fails closed.

Each filtered admission, each continuation admission, and each policy request is rate-limited separately. Logs may record the invocation id, the service, and credential key names. They must not record hop JWTs, session tokens, or credential values.

## Proposals

Agents cannot author a filter. An explicit `filter` key, including `null`, is 400 at create. Deleting a filtered service is rejected at create and at apply, because the request could fall through to unmatched-host passthrough. `enabled: false` is allowed and is a denial, not a bypass. A proposal may update auth on a filtered service, and the filter is preserved. It may not change that service's host, path, or port.

A proposal is also rejected when its effective unfiltered matcher can win or tie an existing filtered matcher for any request (400 at create, 409 at apply). Overlap uses the real host, port, and path languages, including exact glob intersection, not a string-prefix approximation. Equal priority is rejected so declaration order cannot bypass the filter. This restriction is proposal-only. A vault admin may still author an overlapping unfiltered exception in YAML.

## Non-goals

- In-process plugins, WASM, or a rules language.
- A second client-facing proxy.
- A long-lived filter agent or a stored hop-token secret.
- RFC 9457 Problem Details.
- A dashboard or a `vault service filter` subcommand.
- Changing which service wins a request, or how ordinary unfiltered CONNECT revocation works.
- A configurable hop TTL. It is 30 seconds.
- Hiding filtered services from `/discover`.

items.title: Support splitting the management/mitm features at a host level as well as port
MITM rate-limit denials (CONNECT/forward) are silent — no log, no metric, no request_logs row
items.body:
### Summary

When the MITM proxy denies a `CONNECT` (or absolute-form forward) for
rate-limiting, it writes the 429 and returns **without logging or counting
anything**. TLS handshake failures on the same path *do* log
(`p.logger.Warn("mitm TLS handshake failed", …)`), so a rate-limit denial is
strictly less observable than a handshake error — even though a denial can take
down every client behind a shared ingress IP (see #380).

### Where

- `internal/mitm/connect.go` — `handleConnect`:
  ```go
  if d := p.rateLimit.Check(ratelimit.TierAuth, mitmIPKey(r)); !d.Allow {
      ratelimit.WriteDenial(w, d, "Too many CONNECT attempts")
      return   // no logger call, no metric
  }
  ```
- `internal/mitm/forward.go` — `handleForward` has the identical silent
  `WriteDenial(... "Too many proxy requests")`.

### Impact

During a live incident, the proxy was 429-ing authenticated `CONNECT`s
fleet-wide (#380). From the broker side the outage was **invisible**: no WARN,
and denied `CONNECT`s never reach `forwardHandler`, so there is **no
`request_logs` row** for the target host either. The only evidence was in the
clients (`git`'s "Could not connect to server") and the *absence* of forward
rows. Diagnosis required reproducing the 429 by hand.

### Suggested fix

At each MITM rate-limit denial, log at WARN with the tier, the key (or a
redacted form), and `Retry-After`, matching the existing handshake-failure log.
A counter would be even better — e.g. `agentvault_mitm_ratelimit_denied_total`
by tier/reason — which also slots into the `/metrics` endpoint proposed in #329.
Denials being silent is the specific gap; #329 is the general observability
ask.

items.title: MITM CONNECT flood gate keys on peer IP — behind an ingress/NAT one client 429s everyone's authenticated CONNECTs
items.body:
### Summary

The MITM proxy's auth-tier flood gate keys on the **direct peer IP**
(`mitmIPKey` → `r.RemoteAddr`, `internal/mitm/connect.go`). In the normal
deployment for this product — the broker behind an L4/ingress or serving
sandboxes that egress through NAT — `RemoteAddr` is **not** a tenant identity.
It collapses to a small fixed set of ingress IPs, so the per-IP bucket becomes a
**shared/global bucket**: a handful of bad-credential `CONNECT`s from *one*
client trip a 429 that then rejects the `CONNECT` of **every** client behind the
same ingress IP — a fully-authenticated `git clone` included — until the
5-minute window drains.

### Where

- `internal/mitm/connect.go` — `handleConnect` runs
  `p.rateLimit.Check(ratelimit.TierAuth, mitmIPKey(r))` **before**
  `ParseProxyAuth`, and `mitmIPKey` uses `r.RemoteAddr` only. Its own comment
  notes it deliberately ignores `X-Forwarded-For`.
- `internal/mitm/forward.go` — `handleForward` shares the same key and budget.
- The MITM path never calls the `clientIP()` helper, so
  `AGENT_VAULT_TRUSTED_PROXIES` does **not** apply here (and over a
  TLS-terminating TCP ingress with no PROXY protocol there is no real client IP
  to recover anyway).

### Why `RemoteAddr` is the wrong key here

Two independent reasons, both the default topology:

1. **Behind an ingress/reverse proxy**, the backend's peer is the proxy. With a
   Traefik `IngressRouteTCP` (TLS terminated) into a ClusterIP Service and a
   `hostNetwork` Traefik DaemonSet, the broker sees ~N node IPs for **100% of
   external traffic** — effectively N global buckets for the whole fleet.
2. **Sandboxes egress through NAT** (e.g. a sandbox platform's shared egress),
   so even end-to-end the source IP is shared across unrelated tenants.

Either way, the only sound tenant identity is the credential in
`Proxy-Authorization`, not the peer IP.

### Impact

Reproduced live on a hosted deployment (agent-vault @
`sha256:d7bbbc39…`): a burst of bad-credential `CONNECT`s from one source
flipped the proxy `407 → 429`, after which a **correctly**-authenticated
`CONNECT` from the same source IP was refused with 429. On the affected fleet
this produced ~15 provisioning failures in a day, each surfacing to users as
`git clone … Failed to connect to github.com:443 via <broker> … Could not
connect to server`. Plain-HTTP forward traffic that predates the burst is
unaffected, so it reads as an intermittent, source-specific network fault.

### Suggested fix

Key the flood gate on the **proxy-auth token** rather than the peer IP. The
building blocks already exist:

- `internal/ratelimit/key.go` has `HashToken` and `IPTokenKey(clientIP,
  tokenFromRequest)`, already used for the invite/approval token endpoints in
  `internal/server/server.go`.
- The `Proxy-Authorization` header is present on the `CONNECT` request itself
  (parsed a few lines down by `ParseProxyAuth`), so the token is available to a
  keyer.

Concretely: parse proxy auth first, then gate on `ipt:<peer>:<hash(token)>` (or
`hash(token)` alone). Keep a separate, coarse **per-IP** counter only for
**tokenless/malformed** `CONNECT`s — that is the actual credential-stuffing
vector, and it no longer collaterally denies authenticated tenants. A valid
tenant with a good token never shares a bucket with a noisy neighbour.

Happy to send a PR along these lines if the approach sounds right.

items.title: axios cannot reach https:// upstreams through the broker (400 non-CONNECT) — the unmerged half of #208, and the docs say it works
items.body:
## Summary

`axios` cannot reach an `https://` upstream through the Agent Vault broker. It fails with a broker-generated `400`, on **both GET and POST**, for any host — vaulted or passthrough.

This is the axios half of #208, which was closed unmerged. #208's other half (the `@slack/web-api` body token) shipped as #225's body-substitution surface, but the axios fix did not land, and there is no open issue tracking it.

The docs currently state the opposite in two places, which is what makes this expensive to diagnose.

## Reproduction

Any Node process launched via `agent-vault run` (so the proxy env vars and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` are set):

```js
const axios = require('axios');

// FAILS - 400 from the broker
await axios.get('https://api.example.com/v1/thing');
await axios.post('https://api.example.com/v1/thing', { a: 1 });

// WORKS - Node's own proxy support handles it
await axios.get('https://api.example.com/v1/thing',  { proxy: false });
await axios.post('https://api.example.com/v1/thing', { a: 1 }, { proxy: false });

// WORKS - undici
await fetch('https://api.example.com/v1/thing', { method: 'POST' });
```

Response body from the broker:

```
this endpoint is an HTTP forward proxy; non-CONNECT requests must use
absolute-form URLs (http://host/path). Use CONNECT for https:// upstreams.
```

Measured against `api.firecrawl.dev` on server **v0.39.0**, client Node **v24.14.0**, axios **1.15.2**:

| Client | Result |
|---|---|
| axios GET, default | **400** non-CONNECT |
| axios POST, default | **400** non-CONNECT |
| axios GET, `proxy:false` | 200 |
| axios POST, `proxy:false` | 200 |
| native `fetch` POST | 200 |
| `curl` (all header/body variants) | 200 |

## Cause

axios ships its own proxy implementation. It reads the proxy environment variables and then sends a non-CONNECT request for an `https://` upstream instead of opening a CONNECT tunnel, which the MITM ingress correctly rejects.

**The symptom changed in #213 but the bug did not.** #208 describes axios misreading a TLS-wrapped proxy URL as the origin server and tripping netguard's self-loop block. Since #213 removed proxy TLS wrapping (servers >= 0.23 use plain CONNECT), the same defect now surfaces as the `400 non-CONNECT` above. Anyone comparing the two error strings would reasonably conclude they are unrelated problems. They are not.

## Documentation is currently wrong

Both of these list `axios` among clients that transparently route through the broker, on pages that also state the CONNECT requirement axios violates:

- `docs/agents/protocol` — "every standard HTTP client — `curl`, `fetch`, `requests`, `axios`, the Go stdlib ... transparently routes through the broker"
- `docs/self-hosting/local` — "Any standard HTTP client that honors the proxy env vars (curl, fetch, requests, axios, the Go stdlib, SDKs, CLIs) transparently routes through the broker"

Because the docs assert it works, the failure reads as a CA or connectivity fault. It is neither — TLS has already succeeded by the time the 400 arrives.

One further wrinkle: `docs/agents/protocol` describes `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` as enabling built-in proxy support for `fetch()` and `http.get()`/`https.get()`. axios uses `http.request`, yet `proxy:false` works, so the real coverage is broader than documented.

## A trap worth documenting either way

A CLI can appear to work for some commands and 400 on others, if it uses `fetch` for some code paths and axios for others. The Firecrawl CLI does exactly this (`fetch` for `credit-usage`, axios for `scrape`), which initially looked like a GET-vs-POST distinction. It is not — axios fails on both verbs.

## Suggested fixes, in preference order

1. **Correct the two docs pages.** Cheapest, and removes the misdiagnosis. Even without a code fix, saying "axios needs `proxy: false`" would save users the hunt.
2. **Document the `proxy: false` workaround** next to the client list, with the safety note below.
3. **Reconsider the #208 preload**, or a narrower version not scoped to OpenClaw. This affects any axios-based Node CLI, not just OpenClaw.

## Safety note for anyone implementing the workaround

The review on #208 raised this and it is worth preserving. With `axios.defaults.proxy = false`, axios falls back to `https.globalAgent`, which honors the proxy env vars **only** when Node's built-in support is present (>= 22.7) and enabled. If either is missing, axios does not error — it connects **direct, silently bypassing the broker**: no audit record, no credential injection, and any real local credential is sent to the upstream.

Any documented workaround should therefore carry a version/env guard that fails loud, as #208 concluded. Locally I preload a shim that throws when a proxy is configured that Node cannot honor, and I keep vaulted CLIs on a placeholder credential so that even a bypass fails closed with a 401 rather than leaking a live key.

## Environment

- agent-vault server **0.39.0** (Linux, remote over Tailscale)
- client macOS, Node **v24.14.0**, axios **1.15.2**
- `unmatched_host_policy=passthrough`
- reproduced against both a vaulted host (`bearer` injection) and passthrough hosts

items.title: FR: Support outbound HTTP/SOCKS5 proxy for server-side egress
items.body:
## Use case

I run Agent Vault on my own development machine to avoid the latency of a remote deployment. However, my network environment cannot reach several target services directly — GitHub, for example, is unreachable without going through a local proxy. In this situation the Agent Vault server itself cannot dial any upstream, so the broker is unusable even though the client side (`vault run`) works fine.

I imagine this also applies to corporate networks that mandate an egress proxy.

## Current behavior

Server-side outbound connections are always direct dials, with no way to configure an upstream proxy:

- The MITM proxy's upstream transport (`internal/mitm/proxy.go`) builds an `http.Transport` with `DialContext: netguard.SafeDialContext(...)` and no `Proxy` field, so `HTTPS_PROXY`-style env vars are ignored entirely.
- The OAuth token client (`internal/server/server.go`) goes further and explicitly sets `oauthTransport.Proxy = nil`.
- No env var or CLI flag exists to change this (checked `.env.example` and the env-var reference docs).

I understand this is deliberate: netguard resolves hostnames locally, validates the IPs against the SSRF blocklist, and dials the validated IP to prevent DNS rebinding. Forwarding to an upstream proxy re-delegates resolution to the proxy and weakens that guarantee.

## Workarounds I've considered

None of these are great for my situation, which is why I'm opening this issue:

- **Host-level transparent proxy** (iptables/nftables REDIRECT of outbound traffic): too complex to set up and maintain just for one application, and invisible to Agent Vault when debugging.
- **Docker Compose sidecar doing transparent proxying** (e.g. a sidecar container with its own iptables rules forcing egress through my proxy): avoids touching host network config, and Agent Vault already has a Docker deployment story, but it's still a fair amount of moving parts for a single-user dev setup.
- **Running the server on a remote host with good connectivity**: what I'm trying to avoid due to latency.

## Proposal

Add an opt-in upstream proxy for server egress, e.g. `AGENT_VAULT_UPSTREAM_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:7890` (supporting `http://`/`https://` via CONNECT and ideally `socks5://` via `golang.org/x/net/proxy`), with `NO_PROXY`-style bypass for internal targets.

On the SSRF trade-off, one possible framing is an explicit, operator-configured "unsafe" mode — there's precedent in the codebase with `AGENT_VAULT_ALLOW_PRIVATE_RANGES=true`, which weakens the same protection when the operator knows their deployment calls for it. Concretely:

- Off by default; the default security posture is unchanged.
- When set, netguard validates the **proxy address** instead of the final target.
- A prominent warning is logged at startup, e.g. `upstream proxy configured: target SSRF validation delegated to proxy`.
- Optionally keep local checks for literal-IP targets (including `169.254.169.254`, which is how IMDS is reached in practice), so the most dangerous SSRF target stays blocked even in this mode.

That said, I fully understand if the maintainers feel any weakening of netguard isn't a good fit for the project — in that case feel free to close this and I'll make do with one of the workarounds above. If the direction is acceptable, I'm happy to attempt a PR.

items.title: MITM relay drops the body of a 401 from a substitution-bearing service — Content-Length kept, zero body bytes, empty error_code
items.body:
## Summary

When a proxied upstream answers **401** on a host that matches a **service carrying header substitutions**,
the MITM relay forwards the status line and headers — including the upstream's `Content-Length` — and then
closes the connection without sending a single body byte. The vault's own request log records the exchange
with an **empty `error_code`**, so the truncation is silent. The same service relays 200s and 500s (with
larger bodies) intact, and 401s from hosts with no configured service relay intact, so the trigger is
specifically _401 + matched substitution service_.

## Environment

- `infisical/agent-vault:0.39.0` (latest release at the time of writing; `main` shows no response-relay
  changes since), running as a Compose service, in the context of
  [`toryt/scp-173`](https://bitbucket.org/toryt/scp-173) — a reusable development-container sandbox built
  around this vault — MITM ingress, clients trusting the generated CA.
- One service configured for the affected host: match `dev.example.com` — a bare hostname, no scheme, no
  port, matching the whole host. The bare form is forced by the vault itself: it accepts only four host
  forms and has no `path` field, so composing `host + '/'` for a whole-host match yields
  `dev.example.com/`, which is none of them and is refused with a bare `400`. `auth: passthrough`, three
  credential substitutions with `in: ['header']` (sentinel placeholders in the `Authorization` header,
  substituted for real `Basic` values; `in` declared because the surface defaults to path and query).
- Upstream: an AWS CloudFront distribution fronting an IIS backend.

## Reproduction

Through the proxy, from a client container, no `Authorization` header:

```sh
curl -v https://dev.example.com/server/0/app/userInfo
```

Result:

```text
< HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
< Content-Type: text/html
< Content-Length: 1293
< WWW-Authenticate: Basic
< Server: Microsoft-IIS/10.0
< Via: 1.1 …cloudfront.net (CloudFront)
< X-Amz-Cf-Id: ADXRDxMnpBQkdgKUTpO8ooS5TMrSU75tECFQRCJmCK1bF6u-48Ymxg==
…
curl: (18) transfer closed with 1293 bytes remaining to read
```

The `X-Amz-Cf-Id` above is from a controlled single-request window (2026-08-03T16:55:22Z–16:55:23Z, nothing
else crossing the proxy): it identifies this exact response on the CloudFront side, should the origin's
behavior ever need confirming from there. Note the closure is immediate — status, headers, and close within
about a second — so the proxy is actively ending the connection, not stalling on it.

Control, the identical request from a host **without** the proxy, forced `--http1.1` and default HTTP/2
both: all 1293 bytes received, exit 0, twice. The upstream delivers the complete body to anyone not behind
the vault.

## What narrows the trigger

All rows measured through the same proxy instance with plain `curl`, minutes apart:

| host                         | service configured | status | `WWW-Authenticate` | body delimiter        | outcome                   |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------ | ------ | ------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `dev.example.com`            | yes                | 401    | `Basic`            | `Content-Length` 1293 | **0 bytes, `curl: (18)`** |
| `dev.example.com`            | yes                | 500    | —                  | `Content-Length` 2501 | complete                  |
| `dev.example.com`            | yes                | 500    | —                  | `Content-Length` 2513 | complete                  |
| `dev.example.com`            | yes                | 200    | —                  | `Content-Length` 855  | complete                  |
| `api.github.com`             | no                 | 401    | absent             | `Content-Length` 120  | complete                  |
| `the-internet.herokuapp.com` | no                 | 401    | `Basic realm=…`    | `Content-Length` 15   | complete                  |
| `authenticationtest.com`     | no                 | 401    | `Basic realm=…`    | chunked, 3261 bytes   | complete                  |

Hypotheses this kills:

- **Not the status alone**: unconfigured hosts relay 401 bodies intact.
- **Not the host alone**: the same configured service relays 500 bodies intact.
- **Not `WWW-Authenticate`**: an unconfigured host's 401 carrying that header **with a
  `Content-Length`-delimited body** — the same delimiter as the truncated response — relays intact (the
  herokuapp row; the chunked row widens the evidence across the other relay path).
- **Not body size or a cap**: the surviving 500 bodies (2501, 2513) are larger than the dropped 1293.

## The vault's own log at the moment of truncation

The management API request log for the exact event (`gateway-logs.js`, i.e. `/logs`):

```json
{
    "ingress": "mitm",
    "method": "GET",
    "host": "dev.example.com:443",
    "path": "/server/0/app/userInfo",
    "matched_service": "dev-backend",
    "credential_keys": ["USER_A", "USER_B", "USER_C"],
    "status": 401,
    "latency_ms": 1244,
    "error_code": ""
}
```

No error is recorded, in this entry or anywhere near it. From the vault's own telemetry the relay looks
successful. This entry is the single-request window above — the request log carries no field correlating to
`X-Amz-Cf-Id`, so the match is by timestamp on an otherwise quiet proxy. The `latency_ms` is a second,
independent symptom of the same blindness: the vault believes it spent 1.24 s successfully relaying a body
of which it delivered nothing.

## Impact

- A direct client gets `curl: (18)` — annoying but visible.
- A client behind any Node `http-proxy`-family reverse proxy (Vite dev-server proxies, `http-server`)
  **hangs forever**: those proxies pipe the upstream response and only end the client response on `end`,
  which never comes; the 401 headers are never even flushed. A 30 s client timeout expiring with no status
  is the observable symptom, far from the cause.
- Any workflow that must _fail_ authentication on purpose — negative tests, credential probes — breaks
  precisely on the service the vault brokers.

## Notes on mechanism (speculation, labelled as such)

The trigger shape suggests the response path for a 401 from a service the vault holds credentials for is
special-cased (credential-invalidity detection?) and consumes or discards the body instead of relaying it.
If dropping the body is ever intentional, the honest behaviors would be rewriting `Content-Length`, or
answering an explicit 502 with an `X-Agent-Vault-Proxy-Error` before streaming — the pattern #227
established for the body-cap case — and recording a non-empty `error_code` either way.

## Provenance

This report was researched and written by Claude (Claude Code, Anthropic) — an agent running inside a
sandbox this vault brokers, which makes it one of the product's intended users. The measurements were taken
by two Claude Code sessions on either side of the gateway and by the human operator on the host; the
operator reviewed the report and filed it.

items.title: MITM proxy: clarify or support plain HTTP inside CONNECT for legacy Undici clients
items.body:
## Problem

Agent Vault v0.39.0 supports plain HTTP upstreams through absolute-form
forward-proxy requests after #150. However, clients that tunnel a plain HTTP
target through `CONNECT` still fail.

We hit this with Pi 0.80.2 (and confirmed Pi 0.81.1 has the same dependency):

- Pi creates an Undici `EnvHttpProxyAgent` without setting `proxyTunnel`.
- Pi pins Undici 8.5.0, where `proxyTunnel` defaults to `true`.
- A request to `http://mcp.internal/...` therefore sends `CONNECT mcp.internal:80`,
  receives `200 Connection Established`, and then sends
  cleartext HTTP inside the tunnel.
- Agent Vault's CONNECT handler assumes the tunneled protocol is TLS and starts
  a server-side TLS handshake, which fails with `mitm TLS handshake failed`.

The wire sequence is:

```text
Pi fetch(http://mcp.internal/...)
  -> CONNECT mcp.internal:80
  <- HTTP/1.1 200 Connection Established
  -> POST /... HTTP/1.1          # cleartext, not a TLS ClientHello
  -> Agent Vault TLS handshake fails and closes the connection
```

This is different from #132/#150: that fix handles the standard absolute-form
shape (`POST http://mcp.internal/... HTTP/1.1`), so this request never reaches
the new plain HTTP forward path.

## Upstream client fix

Undici has already corrected its default behavior in
https://github.com/nodejs/undici/pull/5116 (first released in 8.7.0):

- HTTP target: absolute-form forwarding
- HTTPS target: CONNECT
- `proxyTunnel: true`: still available when a caller explicitly wants to
  tunnel HTTP

That behavior follows RFC 9112 section 3.2.2 and matches Agent Vault #150.
Therefore, our preferred long-term fix is for Pi to upgrade Undici (ideally to
8.8.x) rather than requiring an Agent Vault change.

## Compatibility request

Would supporting cleartext HTTP inside CONNECT be in scope as a compatibility
fallback for clients pinned to older Undici versions or explicitly using
`proxyTunnel: true`?

A possible implementation would peek and preserve the first tunneled bytes:

- TLS ClientHello: keep the current CONNECT/TLS MITM path.
- Valid HTTP/1.1 request: serve the tunnel as cleartext and reuse #150's
  forwarding path, including host policy, credential injection, header
  stripping, netguard, limits, and request logging.
- Anything else: reject/close rather than treating every non-TLS protocol as
  HTTP.

RFC 9110 section 9.3.6 does not require a CONNECT tunnel to contain TLS, so this
is technically valid, but it should remain a compatibility path rather than the
recommended shape for ordinary HTTP proxy requests.

If this is intentionally out of scope, documenting the requirement for
absolute-form HTTP requests (for example, Undici >= 8.7.0 or
`proxyTunnel: false`) and adding an actionable hint to the TLS-handshake-failure
log would also resolve the ambiguity.

## Self-signed HTTPS alternative considered

We also considered changing the internal endpoint to HTTPS with a self-signed
certificate and adding a global upstream TLS skip-verification switch. I do not
think global `InsecureSkipVerify` is a good fit for a credential broker: Agent
Vault injects the real credential before connecting upstream, so disabling
certificate-chain and hostname verification would expose it to an active MITM.

The safer dev/private-PKI path is to add the internal CA to the Agent Vault
server process trust store. On Linux, the current Go transport can use a system
trust-store installation or `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR` without a code
change. An `SSL_CERT_FILE` bundle should contain both the normal system roots
and the internal CA. A documented, append-only
`AGENT_VAULT_UPSTREAM_CA_FILE` option could make this clearer and avoid
replacing the system bundle, but it is a separate enhancement from cleartext
CONNECT support.

## References

- Agent Vault HTTP support: #132, #150
- Agent Vault v0.39.0 CONNECT handler:
  https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/v0.39.0/internal/mitm/connect.go#L102-L136
- Pi 0.81.1 still pins Undici 8.5.0:
  https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v0.81.1/packages/coding-agent/package.json
- Pi dispatcher:
  https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/blob/v0.81.1/packages/coding-agent/src/core/http-dispatcher.ts
- Undici root cause/fix: https://github.com/nodejs/undici/issues/5093,
  https://github.com/nodejs/undici/pull/5116
- RFC 9110 CONNECT: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-9.3.6
- RFC 9112 absolute-form: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#section-3.2.2
