items.title: Credential version history and rollback for the built-in credential store
items.body:
## Problem

Per the [credentials doc](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/learn/credentials): "If `STRIPE_KEY` already exists, it is overwritten." There's no history and no rollback for the built-in credential store — if an operator (or an agent proposing a `value` back into a credential slot) overwrites a key with a bad value, the previous value is just gone. The only recovery path is remembering it yourself.

This stands out because Infisical's own core platform explicitly ships secret versioning and point-in-time recovery as a headline feature — Agent Vault's built-in store doesn't have an equivalent yet, even though it's conceptually the same "encrypted key/value with mutation history" problem.

(Vaults backed by the [Infisical credential store](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/learn/credential-stores) are out of scope here — Infisical is already the source of truth and has its own versioning. This is specifically for the **built-in** store.)

## Proposal

- Add an append-only `credential_versions` table: on every `set`/overwrite of a built-in credential, write the previous encrypted value + timestamp + actor before applying the new one. Same AES-256-GCM-at-rest treatment as live credentials — no change to the encryption model.
- Bound retention the same way request logs already are (`AGENT_VAULT_LOGS_MAX_AGE_HOURS` / `_MAX_ROWS_PER_VAULT` — following that existing pattern rather than inventing a new one), e.g. `AGENT_VAULT_CREDENTIAL_HISTORY_MAX_VERSIONS` (default something small like 10).
- New CLI/API surface:
  - `agent-vault vault credential history <key> --vault my-vault` — list past versions with timestamp + actor (not the value, unless `--reveal` and sufficient permissions, mirroring `credential list --reveal`'s existing access rule).
  - `agent-vault vault credential rollback <key> --version N --vault my-vault` — restores a prior version as the current value (itself recorded as a new version, so rollback is never destructive).
- Delete (`credential delete`) could optionally also just be a version-preserving soft-delete rather than a hard delete, to match — happy to scope that separately if it adds too much surface to the first PR.

## Why this is worth doing

This is a real "oops" risk today with zero mitigation, and it's a natural feature-parity gap with a capability Infisical already knows works well on the main platform — this isn't proposing something novel, just extending an existing, proven pattern down into Agent Vault's simpler built-in store.

Happy to implement — would start with the versions table + `history`/`rollback` CLI and API endpoints, gated behind the same permission model as `credential get`/`--reveal` (member/admin only, never proxy-role agents).

items.title: Add a Prometheus /metrics endpoint for proxy and system observability
items.body:
## Problem

`agent-vault` is meant to be deployed as its own trust boundary — a separate service sitting in front of every credentialed request an agent makes (per the README: "deploy Agent Vault on a separate machine from your AI agents"). For something running as production infrastructure, there's currently no metrics export of any kind.

Looking through the [environment variables reference](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/self-hosting/environment-variables), there's a lot of operational configuration already (rate-limit tiers, request-log retention, DB pool sizing) but the only runtime visibility into what the proxy is actually doing is:

- `AGENT_VAULT_LOG_LEVEL=debug`, which adds one text log line per proxied request, or
- querying the internal request-log table directly (capped by `AGENT_VAULT_LOGS_MAX_AGE_HOURS` / `AGENT_VAULT_LOGS_MAX_ROWS_PER_VAULT`).

Neither of those wires into Prometheus/Grafana/Datadog, which makes it hard to alert on things operators would actually care about — e.g. a spike in netguard-blocked requests (possible SSRF attempt), rate-limit rejections climbing, or proposal backlog growing.

## Proposal

Add a `/metrics` endpoint (standard `promhttp` handler) on the management API, behind the same auth/network posture as the rest of the management surface. Initial counters/histograms would mostly just be instrumenting things that already exist internally rather than adding new logic:

- `agent_vault_proxy_requests_total{service, status}` — proxied request outcomes
- `agent_vault_proxy_request_duration_seconds` — latency histogram
- `agent_vault_netguard_blocked_total{reason}` — private-range / metadata-endpoint denials (from the existing [network guard](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/learn/security#network-security))
- `agent_vault_ratelimit_rejected_total{tier}` — 429s by tier (`AUTH`, `AUTHED`, `PROXY`, `GLOBAL`)
- `agent_vault_proposals_pending` / `agent_vault_proposals_total{status}` — proposal backlog and lifecycle counts

Could gate it behind an env var (e.g. `AGENT_VAULT_METRICS_ENABLED=true`) to keep it opt-in for anyone who doesn't want the extra endpoint exposed.

## Why this is worth doing

This closes a real gap for anyone running Agent Vault as actual infrastructure rather than a local dev tool — which is exactly how the docs recommend deploying it. It's additive instrumentation on top of existing counters/events, not new business logic, so it should be reviewable in relatively contained pieces (e.g. proxy metrics first, netguard/rate-limit metrics as a follow-up).

Happy to take a first pass at this if it's something you'd want — would start with the proxy request counters/histogram and the `/metrics` endpoint scaffolding, then layer on netguard and rate-limit counters.

items.title: Outbound notifications (Slack/Discord/webhook) for pending proposals
items.body:
## Problem

When an agent raises a [proposal](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/learn/proposals) (e.g. requesting access to a new service), the only notification channels today are:

1. A link shared directly in the agent's chat session, and
2. An email to vault members, if SMTP is configured.

There's no way to route this to a team channel. Proposals expire after a 7-day TTL, and in practice a lot of teams don't have SMTP configured or don't watch that inbox closely — if nobody happens to be in the agent's chat session when the proposal is raised, it can silently sit until it expires, stalling the agent for no reason the operator is aware of.

## Proposal

Add outbound webhook-based notifications for proposal lifecycle events, following the same "env var enables it" pattern already used for SMTP (`AGENT_VAULT_SMTP_*`):

- `AGENT_VAULT_NOTIFY_WEBHOOK_URL` — generic webhook, POSTs a JSON payload (proposal id, vault, agent, requested services/credential slots, approval URL) on `proposal.created`.
- Optionally, a documented Slack-compatible payload shape so operators can point the same env var at an Incoming Webhook URL with zero extra config (Discord's webhook API is also close enough to work with the same generic shape, or with a `AGENT_VAULT_NOTIFY_FORMAT=slack|discord|generic` switch if the payload shapes diverge too much).
- Fire on `proposal.created`; optionally also on `proposal.expiring_soon` (e.g. 24h before the 7-day TTL elapses) so operators get a second nudge before it's gone.

This is intentionally scoped as a notification side-channel only — it doesn't touch credential handling, the proxy path, or the approval/auth flow, so the risk surface is small.

## Why this is worth doing

Agent Vault's core UX loop depends on a human noticing and approving a proposal quickly. Email-only (and often not even configured) is a real gap for teams that live in Slack/Discord, which is presumably most of the target audience for a tool built around AI coding agents.

Happy to implement this if it's a direction you'd want — wanted to check in first since it touches the proposal lifecycle. Would probably start with a generic webhook payload + docs, and layer Slack/Discord formatting on top if useful.

items.title: Restrict a service to specific HTTP methods (read-only credential brokering)
items.body:
## Summary

Add an optional `methods` field to a service so the credential is attached only to requests using the listed HTTP methods. `methods: [GET, HEAD]` would broker a privileged token read-only.

## Motivation

A service today matches on host + optional port + optional path glob. Any matching request gets the credential, whatever the verb. For most resource-oriented REST APIs, path scoping can't express "read-only": the read and the mutation share a path and differ only by method. On api.github.com, `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}` and `DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}` are the same path.

Where the upstream offers a scoped credential (GitHub fine-grained PATs, Stripe restricted keys), that's the better place to enforce read-only. But plenty of internal and legacy REST services issue only an all-or-nothing token. For those, short of trusting the agent's prompt, a method check at the proxy is the only read-only control available.

## Proposal

```yaml
services:
  - name: github-readonly
    host: api.github.com
    methods: [GET, HEAD]
    auth:
      type: bearer
      token: GITHUB_TOKEN
```

- `methods` omitted = all methods, so every existing config keeps its behavior. Validation rejects an explicit `methods: []` rather than treating it as "allow everything."
- Values are uppercase-normalized on ingest and validated against `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `OPTIONS`. The request method is compared case-sensitively against that normalized set. An odd-cased method fails closed.
- A request whose method isn't listed is denied, and the credential is not attached as a header or through substitutions (see Design notes).

**Separable add-on: method-override stripping.** To hold up against upstreams that honor method-override, a service with `methods` set should also strip `X-HTTP-Method-Override` / `X-Method-Override` / `X-HTTP-Method` and the `_method` query parameter before forwarding. Stripping modifies the request, which the `methods` field alone does not, so treat it as a separate yes/no. It's proposed in scope and on by default here, but splits cleanly into a follow-up. It only removes those spoofing tokens; it is not a general header or query matcher. The `_method` body form would need body inspection and stays out of scope.

## Design notes

`methods` adds no new matcher tier. `MatchService` still selects the single most-specific host/port/path winner exactly as today. The method check then runs on that winner, parallel to the existing `IsEnabled()` check in `internal/brokercore/credential.go`: a winner whose list excludes the method is denied outright, with no fall-through to a broader sibling.

The check has to happen at the `Inject` boundary, before either credential path runs. `Inject` resolves both the auth header and any `substitutions`, and substitutions can write the secret into the path, query, or body (they resolve for `passthrough` services too). A header-only check would still leak the credential through substitutions on a request it was supposed to deny.

The check also binds the winning service, not the host. A more specific sibling without `methods` (say `path: /repos/*`) out-matches a broad `methods: [GET]` rule and injects on any verb. Making a whole host read-only means putting `methods` on every overlapping service.

The core plumbing is small: `Methods []string` on `broker.Service` plus validation, and passing `r.Method` into `Inject` — cheap because both call sites in `forwardRequest` already hold it. The rest is trailing surfaces: services API validation, web UI form, agent proposal flow, SDKs, docs. Happy to contribute the PR if the shape is agreeable.

## Limitations

Method checking constrains plain HTTP request semantics, and only that. A WebSocket handshake is a `GET`, so a `methods: [GET]` service still matches it, and a `websocket`-surface substitution writes the credential into frames that carry no method at all. Upstreams that read `_method` from a POST body (Rack, Symfony) can still be spoofed, since that would take body inspection. GraphQL-style POST-everything APIs get nothing from this for the same reason.

## Open questions

Denial status: every broker-policy denial today is 403 (`StatusForbidden` in `internal/brokercore/brokercore.go`), so leaning 403 for consistency. 405 + `Allow` is more literally correct but would be the ingress's first non-403 broker denial.

Per-method credential splitting (GET gets a read token, POST a write token on the same host) is a different mechanism, a selection-time filter rather than a check on the selected winner, and is not part of this ask.

items.title: docs: improve the "Services" learn page (learn/services.mdx)
items.body:
## Summary

The [Services learn page](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault/blob/main/docs/learn/services.mdx) is detailed but dense, and a few things are hard to find or missing. This issue collects concrete improvements to make it easier to skim and act on.

## Suggested improvements

- **Add a consolidated auth-type reference table.** The five auth types (`bearer`, `basic`, `api-key`, `custom`, `passthrough`) are each documented in prose. A single table summarizing type → header(s) set → required fields → optional fields → when to use would let readers pick the right one at a glance before diving into examples.

- **Add a "Troubleshooting / gotchas" section.** Common failure modes are scattered through the page (or absent). Worth pulling together: why a service isn't matching, `403` vs. plain-proxy behavior and `unmatched_host_policy=deny`, the `400` when a referenced credential key is missing, and the `409 multiple services match host` case when a bare host maps to several path-scoped services.

- **Explain how to verify/test a service matches** before relying on it — e.g. what `/discover` returns and how to reason about the matching-priority rules with a concrete request, so users can debug precedence without trial and error.

- **The Substitutions section is long and easy to get lost in.** The `in:` surface scoping is the security boundary and deserves to stand out more (callout + a short "pick the narrowest surface" rule of thumb). A small diagram of request → match → inject/substitute → forward would help.

- **Cross-link from the quickstarts and guides.** The quickstart pages configure services implicitly; adding a "learn more about Services" link back to this page would improve discoverability.

- **Clarify the `name` vs. `host` addressing rules up front.** The rules for when `name` can be omitted (unique `host` + `path` match, legacy auto-slugify) are correct but appear in multiple places; a short note near the top would reduce repetition.

## Why

Services are central to how Agent Vault brokers credentials, so this page is high-traffic for new users. Small structural additions (reference table, troubleshooting, verification steps) would meaningfully lower the time-to-first-working-service.

---

items.title: Proxy does not support dual-stack outbound — IPv6 CONNECT fails when client connects via IPv4
items.body:
## Description

The Agent Vault proxy listens on `*:14322` (dual-stack), but outbound address family is tied to how the client connected:

| Client connects via | IPv4 outbound | IPv6 outbound |
|---------------------|:---:|:---:|
| `127.0.0.1:14322` | ✅ Works | ❌ Fails (HTTP 000) |
| `[::1]:14322` | ❌ Fails | ✅ Works |

When a client connects over IPv4 and requests an IPv6 destination via CONNECT, the proxy fails to establish the outbound connection. This means `HTTPS_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:14322` breaks all IPv6 traffic through the proxy.

## Steps to Reproduce

```bash
# IPv6 through IPv4 proxy — FAILS
curl -6 --proxy http://user:pass@127.0.0.1:14322 https://google.com/
# → HTTP 000 (curl error 7: failed to connect)

# IPv6 through IPv6 proxy — WORKS
curl -6 --proxy http://user:pass@[::1]:14322 https://google.com/
# → HTTP 301
```

## Expected Behavior

The proxy should support dual-stack outbound regardless of which address family the client used to reach it. If a client connected via IPv4 requests an IPv6 destination, the proxy should establish an IPv6 outbound connection.

## Environment

- Agent Vault v0.36.1
- Linux arm64, Debian 13
- Dual-stack VPS with both IPv4 and IPv6 connectivity

## Workaround

Use `--noproxy *` for IPv6-specific requests, or switch the proxy URL to `[::1]` (but that breaks IPv4 outbound). Neither is a real solution.

## Context

The `agent-vault run` wrapper sets `NO_PROXY` on the child to a fixed `localhost,127.0.0.1,<broker_ip>` (confirmed: a pre-set `NO_PROXY` is ignored; `agent-vault run --help` lists no flag to customize it).

## Request

A flag or env var (e.g. `AGENT_VAULT_NO_PROXY` / `--no-proxy`) to extend the bypass list, or have the wrapper merge the pre-set `NO_PROXY` with its defaults rather than overwriting it.

## Workaround currently in use

Patching the wrapped application to use `127.0.0.1` for its in-container client URL (see related Hermes issue).

items.title: feat: automatic command shimming via `agent-vault wrap` and `unwrap`
items.body:
## Summary

Introduce two new CLI subcommands to Agent Vault:
- `agent-vault wrap {COMMAND}`
- `agent-vault unwrap {COMMAND}`

This allows automatic shimming of command-line tools to transparently run through Agent Vault, without requiring the user to prefix every execution with `agent-vault run --`.

## Problem

Today, developers or orchestrators who want to force tool invocations through Agent Vault have to prefix their CLI executions:
```bash
agent-vault run -- claude-code
```
Or manually manage shell scripts, alias configurations, or wrap path environments. 

For some developer environments or background task runners where users have existing scripts or integrated IDE paths that invoke commands directly (e.g., `git`, `claude`, `codex`), having to modify all invocation points to prefix `agent-vault run --` is fragile and high-overhead.

## Proposed Solution

Introduce command wrapping/shimming natively inside the `agent-vault` CLI.

### 1. `agent-vault wrap <command>`

This command creates a lightweight shim executable in a dedicated shim directory (e.g., `~/.agent-vault/shims/` or similar path) or directly in a directory prepended to `$PATH` (like `~/.local/bin` or `~/.agent-vault/bin`). 

The shim executable is a small wrapper script or binary that:
1. Calls `agent-vault run -- <command> "$@"` underneath.
2. Forwards all arguments, signals, and exit codes.

The command should also automatically guide the user or configure prepending the shim directory to their `$PATH` if not already present.

### 2. `agent-vault unwrap <command>`

This command removes the shim executable for the specified command, restoring the system's default command resolution.

## Type of Change
- [x] New feature
- [ ] Refactor / cleanup

items.title: Claude Code Remote Control (/rc) fails with 403 under brokered OAuth — bridge.claudeusercontent.com not injected
items.body:
## Summary

Claude Code's **Remote Control** feature (`/remote-control` / `/rc`) cannot connect when Claude Code's OAuth is brokered through agent-vault. The session disconnects with:

```
Remote Control disconnected · Transport closed: server rejected connection (code 403)
```

This affects the brokered-OAuth setup documented in [`guides/oauth-claude-code`](https://docs.agent-vault.dev/guides/oauth-claude-code).

## Root cause

Per the OAuth-for-Claude-Code guide, the broker stores the real OAuth token and replaces the `__PLACEHOLDER__` in `~/.claude/.credentials.json` on the wire **only for three hosts**:

- `api.anthropic.com`
- `platform.claude.com`
- `mcp-proxy.anthropic.com`

Remote Control opens a WebSocket to a **fourth host that is not in that list**:

- `wss://bridge.claudeusercontent.com` (and `wss://bridge-staging.claudeusercontent.com`)

(confirmed by string-inspecting the Claude Code 2.1.x binary; the host resolves and returns `426 Upgrade Required` to a plain GET.)

Because the bridge host isn't brokered, the WS upgrade carries the literal `__PLACEHOLDER__` instead of the real token → the bridge rejects the handshake with **403**. This reproduces in every launch mode: proxied (placeholder not swapped for this host) and unproxied (no injection at all).

## Impact

Brokered OAuth and Claude Code Remote Control are currently mutually exclusive. The only workaround is to abandon brokering for Claude Code's own OAuth (store the real refreshable token on the agent machine and add the bridge host to `NO_PROXY`), which gives up the on-disk-placeholder guarantee the guide is designed to provide.

## Request

Add `bridge.claudeusercontent.com` (and `bridge-staging.claudeusercontent.com`) to the broker's Claude Code OAuth injection set, so the real access token is injected on the RC WebSocket upgrade the same way it is for the three existing hosts — including WebSocket-upgrade `Authorization` header substitution if that path isn't already covered.

Alternatively, expose a config/env var to extend the OAuth-injection host list (none exists today per `self-hosting/environment-variables`), so operators can add the bridge host without a release.

## Environment

- agent-vault `0.30.0` (also checked release notes through `0.36.1` — no mention of RC/bridge)
- Claude Code `2.1.178`
- Brokered OAuth per `guides/oauth-claude-code`

items.title: Add GitHub App credential type for proxy-side installation token injection
items.body:
## Summary

Agent Vault should support GitHub App credentials as a first-class credential type, so proxy-only agents can access GitHub without ever receiving a GitHub token, private key, or PEM material.

## Problem

Today Agent Vault can inject static credentials and OAuth credentials at proxy time. That works for PATs, API keys, and OAuth access tokens, but GitHub App installation authentication has a different lifecycle:

1. Store GitHub App identity and private key.
2. Sign a short-lived GitHub App JWT.
3. Exchange it for an installation access token.
4. Inject that installation token into proxied GitHub API/git requests.
5. Refresh before expiry.

Without native support, users must either:

- give agents a token outside Agent Vault,
- store a static PAT instead of using GitHub App identity,
- or run a separate broker/rotator beside Agent Vault.

For security-sensitive agent workflows, the desired model is that the agent has only a proxy-role Agent Vault token. It can use allowed GitHub operations through the proxy, but cannot read or exfiltrate the GitHub App private key or derived installation token.

## Proposed Feature

Add a GitHub App credential type that can be referenced by services similarly to static/OAuth credentials.

The generated installation token should be cached server-side until near expiry and refreshed automatically. Proxy-role agents should never be able to read either the source private key or the derived installation token.

This should ideally work for both built-in Agent Vault credentials and Infisical-backed vaults, so teams can keep Infisical as the source of truth for the GitHub App private key while Agent Vault handles derived token minting and proxy-side injection.

items.title: Support serving the web UI under a URL path prefix (e.g. /agent-vault/) behind a reverse proxy
items.body:
## Problem

The server assumes it is mounted at the domain root. Deployers who want Agent Vault on a shared domain under a sub-path (e.g. `https://example.com/agent-vault/`) currently have to use a content-rewriting reverse proxy. A working nginx config today needs all of the following `sub_filter` hacks against the built bundle:

- rewrite `href="/`, `src="/`, `action="/`, and `url(/` in HTML/CSS to the prefix
- rewrite API calls inside the minified JS bundle: `"/v1/`, `'/v1/`, and template-literal `\`/v1/` occurrences
- inject the router basepath by rewriting the minified TanStack Router init (e.g. `Lr({routeTree:` → `Lr({basepath:"<prefix>",routeTree:`), which breaks whenever a rebuild changes minified identifiers
- append a manual `?v=` cache-bust token to .js/.css references, because the rewritten content no longer matches the content-hashed immutable filenames

This is fragile by construction — every image release can silently break the basepath injection.

## Proposal

First-class support in the server:

- a `--ui-base-path` flag / `AGENT_VAULT_UI_BASE_PATH` env var, default "" = current root behavior unchanged
- the server serves UI **and** `/v1` API under the prefix; the proxy passes the path through unmodified (no rewriting)
- runtime injection: the server templates only the unhashed `index.html` (`<base href>`) at startup; the SPA derives its router basepath and API prefix from it, so one published image works for any prefix and hashed assets stay byte-identical for immutable caching
- cookie `Path`, login redirects, invite/approval links, OAuth redirects, and the `av_addr` handed to agents respect the prefix
- docs with a rewrite-free nginx location block

I have a working implementation with tests and docs; PR incoming.

items.title: AUTH rate limit on CONNECT tunnels breaks remote agents (Docker, VPS)
items.body:
## Problem

Remote agents (Docker containers, VPS deployments) get `429 Too Many Requests` on the MITM proxy after ~10 HTTPS connections, blocking all proxy traffic for 5 minutes. The error surfaces in client libraries as `Connection error` or `APIConnectionError` with no indication it's a rate limit, making it very hard to diagnose.

## Root Cause

`internal/mitm/connect.go:53-57` — every CONNECT tunnel through the MITM proxy counts against the `TierAuth` rate limit (10 per 5 min per IP). The check runs **before** proxy authentication:

```go
func (p *Proxy) handleConnect(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Gate before ParseProxyAuth + session lookup so a bad-auth flood
    // can't burn CPU. Per-IP on the raw TCP peer, shared with the
    // TierAuth budget. Loopback is exempt — see isLoopbackPeer.
    if p.rateLimit != nil && !isLoopbackPeer(r) {
        if d := p.rateLimit.Allow(ratelimit.TierAuth, mitmIPKey(r)); !d.Allow {
            ratelimit.WriteDenial(w, d, "Too many CONNECT attempts")
            return  // ← 429 here, never reaches authentication on line 74
        }
    }

    // ... 15 lines later ...

    // Authenticate the CONNECT request via Proxy-Authorization
    token, hint, err := brokercore.ParseProxyAuth(r)  // line 74
```

The `TierAuth` tier was designed to prevent login brute-force (10 attempts per 5 min is appropriate for password guessing). But CONNECT tunnels also count against this same budget.

**Loopback (127.0.0.1) is already exempt** — the code acknowledges that agents "legitimately open dozens of CONNECTs on startup" (comment on line 29-35). But remote agents (Docker containers, VPS deployments) are not exempt, and they hit the exact same problem.

## How an Agent Exhausts the Budget

A typical agent (e.g., Hermes with Discord) opens these CONNECT tunnels on startup:

1. `discord.com` — REST API login
2. `gateway.discord.gg` — WebSocket connection
3. `api.anthropic.com` — main LLM client
4. `api.anthropic.com` — auxiliary client (title generation)
5. `api.anthropic.com` — auxiliary client (summarization)
6. Any reconnects or retries from transient errors

That's 5-6 tunnels immediately. One user message triggers a few more (streaming creates new connections in some HTTP clients). After 10 total, the proxy returns 429 on every new CONNECT for the remaining 5-minute window.

## What the User Sees

The 429 happens at the CONNECT level (before TLS), so HTTP client libraries don't see it as a rate limit — they see a failed tunnel establishment. Examples:

- **Python (httpx/Anthropic SDK):** `anthropic.APIConnectionError: Connection error.`
- **Python (aiohttp/discord.py):** `aiohttp.ClientHttpProxyError: 429, message='Too Many Requests'`
- **Go:** `bad gateway` or connection refused

No `Retry-After` header reaches the application layer because the CONNECT response is consumed by the HTTP client's proxy handling, not exposed to the application.

## Discovered During

Testing the body + WebSocket substitution feature (#209) with Hermes + Discord in Docker. Took several hours to diagnose because the error message gives no hint it's a rate limit. The Hermes-on-VPS guide already tells users to disable rate limiting entirely as a workaround, which confirms this is a known pain point.

## Suggested Fix

**Minimal (recommended):** Don't count CONNECT tunnels against `TierAuth` when proxy authentication succeeds. The `TierProxy` tier (20 req/s, burst 200, 64 concurrent) already rate-limits authenticated proxy traffic appropriately. The AUTH check on CONNECT should only fire when authentication **fails** — that's the actual brute-force vector it was designed to prevent.

Concretely, in `connect.go`: move the `TierAuth` rate limit check to after `ParseProxyAuth` and `ResolveForProxy`, and only apply it on auth failure. On auth success, skip the AUTH tier entirely.

**Broader improvement (optional, can be a follow-up):** Consider removing `TierProxy` and `TierAuthed` from the default profile entirely. Agent Vault is typically deployed on private networks where the agent already authenticates with a token — rate limiting authenticated traffic protects against a threat that doesn't exist in most deployments. Keep `TierAuth` on login/register (real brute-force risk if API is internet-exposed), `TierGlobal` as a server-wide safety net, and `TierVerifyFail` for verification codes. Operators who want tighter limits can switch to the `strict` profile.

## Current Rate Limit Tiers (for context)

| Tier | Where | What it limits | Default | Issue? |
|------|-------|---------------|---------|--------|
| **AUTH** | API + Proxy CONNECT | Login, register, forgot-password, AND CONNECT tunnels | 10 per 5 min per IP | **Yes — breaks remote agents** |
| **PROXY** | Proxy only | Forwarded requests after authentication | 20 req/s, burst 200, 64 concurrent | No, but unnecessary for private networks |
| **AUTHED** | API only | Authenticated API calls (proposals, vaults, credentials) | 10 req/s, burst 240 | No, but unnecessary — session is the protection |
| **GLOBAL** | Everything | Server-wide backstop | 2000 req/s, 512 concurrent | No — keep as safety net |
| **VERIFY_FAIL** | API only | Bad verification/reset code guesses | 10 bad guesses, code burned | No — keep for brute-force protection |

## Workaround

Until fixed, users can crank up the AUTH tier via the admin API:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:14321/v1/admin/settings \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"rate_limit": {"overrides": {"AUTH": {"window": "1m", "max": 10000}}}}'
```

Or disable rate limiting entirely (what the Hermes guide currently recommends):

```bash
# Via UI: Manage Instance → Rate Limiting → Off
# Via env: set profile to "off" in admin settings
```

## Files to Look At

- `internal/mitm/connect.go` — CONNECT handler, lines 49-58 (the rate limit check), lines 74-83 (authentication)
- `internal/mitm/forward.go` — forward-proxy handler has the same pattern (search for `TierAuth`)
- `internal/ratelimit/` — tier definitions, defaults, algorithms
- `internal/server/ratelimit_settings.go` — how settings are stored and applied

items.title: Support explicit WebSocket frame substitutions for credentials in post-upgrade protocols
items.body:
# Support explicit WebSocket frame substitutions for credentials in post-upgrade protocols

## Problem

Agent Vault substitutions currently work for HTTP request surfaces (`path`, `query`, `header`) before a request is forwarded. This works for REST APIs and for WebSocket handshake metadata, but it does not work for credentials sent inside WebSocket message frames after the HTTP upgrade.

This breaks Discord Gateway auth for Hermes Agent when the Discord bot token is stored in Agent Vault as a substitution placeholder.

**Discord auth flow:**

1. Client opens a WebSocket to Discord Gateway.
2. HTTP/WebSocket handshake succeeds through Agent Vault.
3. Client sends an Identify payload over the established WebSocket.
4. The bot token is inside the JSON WebSocket message body, e.g. `d.token`.
5. Agent Vault currently raw-pipes WebSocket bytes after upgrade, so the placeholder is not substituted.
6. Discord closes the Gateway connection with auth failure.

## Reproduction

**Environment:**

- Agent Vault with MITM proxy enabled
- Hermes Agent gateway running under Agent Vault proxy env
- Discord configured as a Hermes messaging platform
- `DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN` stored as an Agent Vault credential
- Hermes configured with placeholder token: `__discord_bot_token__`

**Services configured in Agent Vault:**

```yaml
discord-api:
  host: discord.com/api/*
  auth: passthrough
  substitution:
    placeholder: __discord_bot_token__
    credential: DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN
    surface: header

discord-gateway:
  host: gateway.discord.gg
  auth: passthrough
  substitution:
    placeholder: __discord_bot_token__
    credential: DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN
    surface: header
```

**Systemd user service was configured to load Agent Vault proxy env:**

```ini
[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/root/.hermes/gateway.env
```

**Manual REST check succeeds** when the placeholder is in an HTTP header:

```bash
set -a
. /root/.hermes/gateway.env
set +a

curl --proxy-cacert /root/.agent-vault/mitm-ca.pem \
  --cacert /root/.agent-vault/mitm-ca.pem \
  -sS -o /tmp/discord_me.out -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  https://discord.com/api/users/@me \
  -H 'Authorization: Bot __discord_bot_token__'

cat /tmp/discord_me.out
```

**Observed result:**

```
HTTP 200
{"id":"...","username":"bot-test", ...}
```

This confirms Agent Vault substituted the placeholder correctly for the HTTP REST request.

**Then restarting Hermes Gateway fails at the Discord Gateway stage:**

```bash
systemctl --user restart hermes-gateway
journalctl --user -u hermes-gateway -n 80 --no-pager
```

**Observed log:**

```
discord.errors.ConnectionClosed: Shard ID None WebSocket closed with 4004
```

Discord close code `4004` indicates authentication failure. This is consistent with the Identify WebSocket payload still containing the literal placeholder rather than the real token.

## Root Cause

The WebSocket proxy path upgrades the connection, then raw-copies bytes between client and upstream.

`internal/mitm/forward.go` applies substitutions only before WebSocket forwarding:

```go
brokercore.ApplySubstitutions(outReq.URL, outReq.Header, inject.Substitutions)
```

`internal/mitm/websocket.go` then pipes the WebSocket connection as bytes:

```go
pipeWebSocket(clientConn, clientBuf.Reader, upstreamConn, upstreamReader)
```

So Agent Vault never parses client→upstream WebSocket frames and cannot replace placeholders inside post-upgrade messages.

## Why this matters

Some APIs authenticate inside protocol messages rather than HTTP metadata. Discord Gateway is a concrete example: the bot token is sent in the Identify frame, not the HTTP handshake.

Without WebSocket frame substitution, users cannot keep Discord bot tokens fully inside Agent Vault when using clients that expect to place the token in the Gateway Identify payload.

## Possible Fix

Add an explicit opt-in substitution surface for WebSocket text frames, e.g.:

```yaml
substitutions:
  - key: DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN
    placeholder: __discord_bot_token__
    in: ["ws_text"]
```

**Implementation sketch:**

1. Add `ws_text` to the supported substitution surfaces.
2. Keep existing `path`, `query`, and `header` behavior unchanged.
3. If a matched service has `ws_text` substitutions and the request is a WebSocket upgrade:
   - Do not raw-copy client→upstream bytes.
   - Parse RFC 6455 frames from the client.
   - Unmask client frames.
   - For text messages, replace declared placeholders.
   - Re-frame data to the upstream.
   - Pass binary/control frames through correctly.
4. Apply substitutions only client→upstream, not upstream→client.
5. Add message/frame size limits.
6. Do not log resolved substitution values.
7. Disable or strip `permessage-deflate` for rewritten WebSocket connections initially, unless compression support is implemented. Rewriting compressed frames safely requires decompress/recompress.

A narrower first pass could support text frames only and reject/skip substitution when compression is negotiated.

## Security Considerations

This should be explicit opt-in. Do not scan all WebSocket traffic by default.

The substitution declaration should remain the security boundary, same as existing `path`/`query`/`header` substitutions. Operators must deliberately opt into `ws_text` for a service.

**Potential follow-up:** consider a more structured `ws_json` surface with JSON path targeting, e.g. replacing `$.d.token`, to avoid raw text replacement inside arbitrary JSON. For the Discord use case, raw text replacement of a unique placeholder is sufficient, but JSON-aware substitution may be safer long-term.

items.title: Codex CLI WebSocket transport fails with Agent Vault HTTPS proxy URL
items.body:
## Summary

Codex runs in a separate agent container from Agent Vault. The agent container does not have the real OpenAI key; it only has a dummy `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Agent Vault runs in its own container and injects the real credential through the proxy.

Using the current Codex quickstart model, `agent-vault run -- codex ...` starts Codex successfully and Codex eventually succeeds through HTTP fallback, but Codex's Responses WebSocket transport still fails first with:

```text
ERROR codex_api::endpoint::responses_websocket: failed to connect to websocket: URL error: Proxy URL scheme not supported, url: wss://api.openai.com/v1/responses
```

## Setup

Two separate containers on the same Docker network:

- `agent-vault` container: `infisical/agent-vault:latest`, exposes control API on `14321` and MITM proxy on `14322`.
- `codex-agent` container: `node:24-bookworm-slim`, with `codex-cli 0.131.0` and `/usr/local/bin/agent-vault` copied from `infisical/agent-vault:latest`.

The Codex container is started with:

```text
AGENT_VAULT_ADDR=http://agent-vault:14321
AGENT_VAULT_TOKEN=av_agt_...
AGENT_VAULT_VAULT=default
OPENAI_API_KEY=dummy-agent-visible-key
```

## Command executed

```sh
agent-vault run -- codex exec --skip-git-repo-check \
  'Reply exactly: docs agent vault run smoke ok'
```

`--skip-git-repo-check` is only needed because the repro runs from a throwaway non-git container directory.

## Observed result

Codex returns the expected output:

```text
docs agent vault run smoke ok
```

But stderr includes repeated Responses WebSocket failures before fallback succeeds:

```text
agent-vault: routing HTTP/HTTPS through MITM proxy (agent-vault:14322)
agent-vault: Installed Agent Vault skills for Codex.
agent-vault: agent-vault connected. Starting codex...
OpenAI Codex v0.131.0
2026-05-20T17:57:11.151374Z ERROR codex_api::endpoint::responses_websocket: failed to connect to websocket: URL error: Proxy URL scheme not supported, url: wss://api.openai.com/v1/responses
```

## Versions tested

- `agent-vault 0.21.0`, commit `fa888ca`, built `2026-05-19T14:34:31Z`
- `codex-cli 0.131.0`

The same error also reproduced on `agent-vault 0.15.0`.

## Other checks

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Node `ws` + `HttpsProxyAgent` through Agent Vault | WSS opens successfully |
| `agent-vault run -- codex exec ...` | Codex succeeds through fallback, but Responses WebSocket logs `Proxy URL scheme not supported` |
| No proxy env | Fails 401 because agent container only has dummy visible OpenAI key |
| Plain `http://` proxy URL | Fails with `HTTP CONNECT response missing status line` |

## Interpretation

Agent Vault's WSS MITM path works for a normal WebSocket client. The failure appears specific to Codex's Responses WebSocket transport rejecting the proxy URL before it reaches Agent Vault.

items.title: Supply-chain hardening shortlist. Would any of these PRs be welcome?
items.body:
Hi 👋, prospective user here doing a pre-adoption security review of `agent-vault`. I spent a few hours auditing the CI/CD setup, release pipeline, and install path, especially in light of recent supply-chain incidents.

Before I send anything as PRs, I wanted to check which (if any) you'd welcome. Each proposal below is self-contained and each would be a separate small PR.

## Small PRs I'd happily send

1. **Dependabot cooldown** — catches freshly-published malicious versions before they land in auto-PRs.
2. **`npm install` → `npm ci` in `release-node-sdk.yml`** — installs strictly from the lockfile, closing the window between what CI tested and what ships to npm (vector the Axios compromise exploited).
3. **`npm ci --ignore-scripts` + `npm rebuild esbuild`** across all npm install steps — blocks arbitrary `postinstall` execution in transitive deps, while still letting esbuild fetch its platform binary.
4. **Downgrade `contents: write` → `contents: read`** on the node-sdk publish workflow — checkout needs `contents: read`; OIDC publish needs `id-token: write`; nothing in the job writes to the repo.
5. **`persist-credentials: false`** on `actions/checkout` — found by `zizmor` (artipacked). No `git` command happens in any workflow, so the `GITHUB_TOKEN` doesn't need to be left in `.git/config`.
6. **`--proto '=https'`** on `install.sh` curl calls — defense-in-depth against HTTP redirect downgrade.
7. **Pin Dockerfile base images by digest** and enable Dependabot's `docker` ecosystem — floating tags (`alpine:3.21`, `node:22-alpine`, `golang:1.25-alpine`) are mutable upstream; a retag or compromise lands silently in the next build. Digest pinning (`@sha256:...`) makes base-image changes opt-in; the Dependabot docker ecosystem keeps the pins fresh so they don't rot.
8. **`actions/attest-build-provenance` after GoReleaser** — enables `gh attestation verify agent-vault_*.tar.gz --repo Infisical/agent-vault` for users with zero extra tool install.
9. **`docker_signs` block in `.goreleaser.yml`** — cosign is already installed in the release workflow; it's currently only used to sign `checksums.txt`.

## Bigger but still small-ish

10. **Checksum + cosign verification in `install.sh`** — the current installer downloads and executes the binary without integrity verification, despite `.goreleaser.yml` already publishing a signed `checksums.txt`. Largest single impact of any change here; happy to send as its own PR after (8) lands so it can prefer `gh attestation verify` when available.

## Things that need maintainer action (flagging, not PR'ing)

These are settings / external-infra changes only you can make. Listing so they're on your radar; happy to defer on any of them:

- **Immutable Releases** (repo settings → Releases) — single checkbox that prevents the Trivy-class (Mar 2026) and tj-actions-class (Mar 2025) asset-swap attacks by making release tags and assets platform-level immutable after publication. Complements cosign by making the platform itself enforce tamper-evidence.
- **Tag protection ruleset** on `v*` / `node-sdk/v*.*.*` pushes with `creation` / `deletion` / `non_fast_forward` rules.
- **DNSSEC on `agent-vault.dev`** — zone is currently unsigned (signed NSEC3 denial from the `dev.` TLD confirmed). One click in Cloudflare + DS record at the registrar. Important given the install-path trust reliance on the domain.

## A few questions before I start

- **Bundling preference** — happy with 10 separate small PRs, or would you rather a couple of "security hardening batch" PRs grouped by concern (e.g. one for Dependabot-related, one for permissions)?
- **Order preference** — I'd suggest starting with 1-6 (truly tiny wins, easy review), then 7-9 (still small, need one look), then 10 (slightly bigger). Open to any order you prefer.
- **Overlap** — if any of this is already planned or WIP on your end, just say so and I'll drop it.

Thanks for the project!

items.title: Add per-service custom-header passthrough for provider APIs that require non-standard headers (e.g., anthropic-version)
items.body:
## Summary

`internal/brokercore/brokercore.go`'s `PassthroughHeaders` allowlist (Content-Type, Content-Encoding, Accept, Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language, User-Agent, Idempotency-Key, X-Request-Id) drops any other client-supplied request headers for credentialed (non-passthrough) services. This breaks provider APIs that require non-standard request headers — most notably **Anthropic's `anthropic-version` header** which is mandatory on every `/v1/messages` request.

## Repro

```bash
agent-vault server -d
# attach api.anthropic.com via API-key auth, x-api-key header, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY credential
agent-vault run --vault default -- curl -s -X POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages \
  -H "anthropic-version: 2023-06-01" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"claude-haiku-4-5","max_tokens":3,"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hi"}]}'
```

Returns:
```
{"type":"error","error":{"type":"invalid_request_error","message":"anthropic-version: header is required"}}
```

The cred injection works (no 401), but `anthropic-version` was dropped during MITM rewriting.

Confirmed via debug log + source review — `PassthroughHeaders` doesn't include `anthropic-version`, so it's stripped in the agent → upstream hop.

## Suggested fix

Add a per-service config field (e.g., `extra_passthrough_headers: ["anthropic-version", "openai-organization", ...]`) so service operators can extend the allowlist for the provider they're brokering for. The catalog templates could pre-fill known-required headers per provider.

## Workarounds tried

- Sending `Anthropic-Version` (capitalized) — also dropped (same allowlist).
- Sending as `X-Anthropic-Version` — dropped.
- Sending as a query param — Anthropic API doesn't accept it that way.

Currently the only workaround is **fork agent-vault** and edit `PassthroughHeaders`, which violates the no-fork stance for adopters.

## Context

I'm adopting agent-vault for a credential brokering layer alongside an egress-policy proxy at SourcePad. The cred-broker is working perfectly otherwise (v0.10.0 commit 2b8e020) — this header-stripping is the one rough edge that makes Anthropic-via-vault fail.

Happy to PR if you want a reviewer's hand on it.

items.title: Potential Path Handling Concern in CLI User Commands
items.body:
hey, while going through the `agent-vault/cmd/user.go`, i noticed that the email input is directly used in constructing API paths
```go
url := sess.Address + "/v1/admin/users/" + email
```
since `email` comes straight from CLI arguments, inputs containing `/` or encoded characters could affect how the final request path is formed

from here, i was thinking this might impact how requests are routed on the backend, especially if path parsing or validation is not strict, it could potentially lead to unintended endpoint access or route confusion

just wanted to check, is this an intentional design choice or am i missing something? would love to help
